claims.claim: The IC50 of cocaine for SERT inhibition at 1 µM 5-HT is 9.8 µM.
claims.source: The IC50(1) was indistinguishable from IC50(0.1) (Figure 1A, blue dashed curve, IC50=9.8 µM, 95% CI: 7.1–13.6)
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake inhibition data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The IC50 of cocaine for SERT inhibition at 10 µM 5-HT is 34.6 µM, representing a ~4-fold right shift.
claims.source: while IC50(10) was right shifted by ~4-fold (Figure 1A, blue dotted curve, IC50=34.6 µM, 95% CI: 24.8–48.3).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake inhibition data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The right shift in cocaine IC50 with increasing serotonin is expected and explained by competitive inhibition.
claims.source: This right shift is expected and readily explained; increasing concentrations of unlabeled 5-HT in the uptake inhibition assay inhibits cocaine binding to SERT in a competitive manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from established competitive inhibition mechanisms.

claims.claim: Noribogaine blocks substrate uptake of SERT more potently in the presence of unlabeled 5-HT.
claims.source: Noribogaine, on the other hand, blocked substrate uptake of SERT more potently in the presence of unlabeled 5-HT (cf. solid, dashed, and dotted green lines, Figure 1B, IC50(0.1): 5.68 µM [95% CI: 4.36–7.39], IC50(1): 2.39 µM [95% CI: 1.84–3.09], IC50(10): 1.89 µM [95% CI: 1.46–2.44]).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake inhibition data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The left shift in potency of noribogaine in the presence of unlabeled 5-HT is more prominent with ECSI#6.
claims.source: In the presence of unlabeled 5-HT, this left shift in potency was more prominent with ECSI#6 (cf. solid, dashed, and dotted red lines, Figure 1B, IC50(0.1): 440.5 µM [95% CI: 325.8–595.6], IC50(1): 74.14 µM [95% CI: 55.4–99.22], IC50(10): 19.28 µM [95% CI: 13.23–28.09]).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake inhibition data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Noribogaine and ECSI#6 bind to SERT with higher affinity in the presence of substrate.
claims.source: These observations clearly show that noribogaine and ECSI#6 bind to SERT with higher affinity in the presence of a substrate.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental uptake inhibition data.

claims.claim: The mode of binding of noribogaine and ECSI#6 to SERT differs from that of cocaine.
claims.source: Thus, their mode of binding to the transporter differs from that of cocaine.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the different patterns of IC50 shifts observed experimentally.

claims.claim: Addition of 1 or 10 µM 5-HT shifted the displacement curve of ECSI#6 for [3H]citalopram binding to the right.
claims.source: It is evident from Figure 2C that addition of 1 or 10 µM 5-HT shifted the displacement curve of ECSI#6 to the right to an extent which was comparable to that seen with cocaine (Figure 2A) and noribogaine (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental radioligand binding data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Dixon plots allow for differentiating mutually exclusive from mutually non-exclusive binding.
claims.source: Thus, Dixon plots allow for differentiating mutually exclusive from mutually non-exclusive binding, if one inhibitor (i.e., cocaine, noribogaine, or ECSI#6) is examined at a fixed concentration of the second inhibitor (i.e., serotonin) (Segel, 1975)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Segel, 1975.

claims.claim: Binding of serotonin and cocaine to SERT is mutually exclusive.
claims.source: It is evident from Figure 2D–E that the presence of 1 and 10 µM serotonin progressively shifted the (expected) x-intercept for cocaine (Figure 2D), noribogaine (Figure 2E), and ECSI#6 (Figure 2D). Thus, binding of serotonin and one of these three ligands to SERT was mutually exclusive.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental Dixon plot analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Binding of serotonin and noribogaine to SERT is mutually exclusive.
claims.source: It is evident from Figure 2D–E that the presence of 1 and 10 µM serotonin progressively shifted the (expected) x-intercept for cocaine (Figure 2D), noribogaine (Figure 2E), and ECSI#6 (Figure 2D). Thus, binding of serotonin and one of these three ligands to SERT was mutually exclusive.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental Dixon plot analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Binding of serotonin and ECSI#6 to SERT is mutually exclusive.
claims.source: It is evident from Figure 2D–E that the presence of 1 and 10 µM serotonin progressively shifted the (expected) x-intercept for cocaine (Figure 2D), noribogaine (Figure 2E), and ECSI#6 (Figure 2D). Thus, binding of serotonin and one of these three ligands to SERT was mutually exclusive.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental Dixon plot analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: K+ promotes the return step of SERT and drives SERT into the outward-facing state.
claims.source: K+ promotes the return step of SERT and thus drives SERT into the outward-facing state.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established mechanistic understanding of SERT transport cycle.

claims.claim: Detectable levels of radioligand binding to SERT can be measured in the presence of 120 mM K+.
claims.source: This allows for measuring detectable levels of radioligand binding in the presence of 120 mM K+ (Bhat et al., 2021c; Schicker et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bhat et al., 2021c and Schicker et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Cocaine is substantially less potent (by an order of magnitude) in inhibiting [3H]citalopram binding in the presence of 120 mM KCl than in the presence of 120 mM NaCl.
claims.source: As expected, cocaine was substantially less potent (by an order of magnitude) in inhibiting [3H]citalopram binding in the presence of 120 mM KCl than in the presence of 120 mM NaCl (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental radioligand binding data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Cocaine binds more readily to Na+-bound SERT.
claims.source: This indicates that cocaine binds more readily to Na+-bound SERT.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the differential potency in Na+ vs K+ conditions.

claims.claim: The distinct binding preference of cocaine for Na+-bound SERT was not obvious with noribogaine.
claims.source: This distinct binding preference was not obvious with noribogaine (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental radioligand binding data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: ECSI#6 is about 10-fold more potent in displacing [3H]citalopram binding in the presence of 120 mM KCl than in the presence of 120 mM NaCl.
claims.source: Importantly and in contrast to cocaine, ECSI#6 was about 10-fold more potent in displacing [3H]citalopram binding in the presence of 120 mM KCl than in the presence of 120 mM NaCl (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental radioligand binding data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: ECSI#6 clearly preferred K+-bound SERT.
claims.source: Thus ECSI#6 clearly preferred K+-bound SERT.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the differential potency in K+ vs Na+ conditions.

claims.claim: Cocaine is a competitive inhibitor of substrate uptake by SERT.
claims.source: Cocaine and noribogaine are competitive and non-competitive inhibitors of substrate uptake by SERT, respectively (Jacobs et al., 2007; Bulling et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jacobs et al., 2007 and Bulling et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Noribogaine is a non-competitive inhibitor of substrate uptake by SERT.
claims.source: Cocaine and noribogaine are competitive and non-competitive inhibitors of substrate uptake by SERT, respectively (Jacobs et al., 2007; Bulling et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jacobs et al., 2007 and Bulling et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Increasing concentrations of ECSI#6 caused a reduction in both KM and VMAX of 5-HT uptake by SERT.
claims.source: This was the case: increasing concentrations of ECSI#6 shifted the saturation hyperbolae for 5-HT uptake (Figure 3C, top) and caused a reduction in both, KM (Figure 3C, middle panel) and VMAX (Figure 3C, bottom panel).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental saturation kinetics data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Reduction in both KM and VMAX is the hallmark of uncompetitive inhibition.
claims.source: This is the hallmark of uncompetitive inhibition.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established enzyme kinetics knowledge.

claims.claim: Cocaine causes a progressive increase in KM values with no change in Vmax values.
claims.source: In the presence of 3 μM (blue squares), 10 μM (blue upward triangles), and 30 μM cocaine (blue downward triangles), there was a progressive increase in KM-values (panel D) with KM = 2.2 µM [95% CI, 1.1–3.3], 3.7 µM [95% CI, 1.9–5.5], and 8.1 µM [95% CI, 1.9–5.5], respectively. The inset in panel D shows the same data on a linear abscissa to visualize the linear relation between apparent KM and cocaine concentration. In contrast to the KM values, the Vmax-values remained constant (panel G, VMAX = 118.3 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 117.4–157.3], 121.1 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 105.5–136.8], and 120.1 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 104.6–135.6], respectively).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental saturation kinetics data shown in Figure 3A, D, and G.

claims.claim: Noribogaine does not change KM values but reduces VMAX in a concentration-dependent manner.
claims.source: Preincubation with 1 µM (yellow squares), 3 μM (yellow upward triangles), and 10 μM noribogaine (yellow downward triangles) did not change the KM-values (panel E with KM = 2.4 µM [95% CI, 1.4–3.5], KM = 1.9 µM [95% CI, 0.6–3.3], and 2.4 µM [95% CI, 0.6–5.5], respectively). The inset shows the same data on a linear abscissa. The VMAX on the other hand was reduced in a concentration-dependent manner (panel H with VMAX = 82.4 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 69.3–95.4], 39.9 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 30.6–49.2], and 19.5 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 13.9–24.9], respectively).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental saturation kinetics data shown in Figure 3B, E, and H.

claims.claim: ECSI#6 leads to a drop in both KM and VMAX values.
claims.source: Preincubation with 10 μM (red squares), 30 μM (red upward triangles), and 100 μM ECSI#6 (red downward triangles) led to a drop in both, the KM-values (panel F, KM = 1.7 µM [95% CI, 0.5–2.9], 1.1 µM [95% CI, 0.2–1.9], and 0.4 µM [95% CI, 0.0–0.8], respectively; the inset shows the same data on a linear abscissa) and the VMAX-values (panel I, VMAX = 89.5 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 68.5–110.0], 49.9 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 37.5–62.3], and 20.8 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 15.6–26.0], respectively).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental saturation kinetics data shown in Figure 3C, F, and I.

claims.claim: The transport cycle of SERT can be addressed by whole-cell patch clamp recordings.
claims.source: The transport cycle of SERT can be addressed by whole-cell patch clamp recordings; electrophysiological recordings of currents through SERT provide unmatched temporal resolution of ligand and co-substrate binding and unbinding events (Hasenhuetl et al., 2016; Hasenhuetl et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hasenhuetl et al., 2016 and Hasenhuetl et al., 2015.

claims.claim: When challenged with a substrate like 5-HT or amphetamines, SERT carries inward currents comprised of an initial transient peak current and a steady current.
claims.source: When challenged with a substrate like 5-HT or amphetamines, SERT carries inward currents. These are comprised of an initial transient peak current and a steady current.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established electrophysiological characterization of SERT.

claims.claim: The peak current reflects the initial synchronized movement of substrate and co-substrate through the membrane electric field.
claims.source: The peak current reflects the initial synchronized movement of substrate and co-substrate through the membrane electric field.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established mechanistic understanding of transporter electrophysiology.

claims.claim: The steady current arises from an uncoupled current and reflects the continuous cycling of the transporter in the forward transport mode.
claims.source: The steady current arises from an uncoupled current; the underlying channel mode is visited from the K+-bound inward-facing state. Thus, the steady current reflects the continuous cycling of the transporter in the forward transport mode (Schicker et al., 2012; Sandtner et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schicker et al., 2012 and Sandtner et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Inhibitors only elicit a minor peak current on application to SERT-expressing cells.
claims.source: In contrast, inhibitors only elicit a minor peak current on application to SERT-expressing cells (Burtscher et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Burtscher et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Cocaine and noribogaine induced transient peak currents, while ECSI#6 failed to do so.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4A, cocaine and noribogaine induced transient peak currents, while ECSI#6 failed to do so.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In the presence of physiological ion gradients and in the absence of substrate, SERT dwells primarily in the outward-facing conformation.
claims.source: In the presence of physiological ion gradients and in the absence of substrate, SERT dwells primarily in the outward-facing conformation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established mechanistic understanding of SERT conformational states.

claims.claim: A precondition for a ligand to elicit a peak current is the ability to bind to outward-facing states.
claims.source: A precondition for a ligand to elicit a peak current is, therefore, the ability to bind to outward-facing states.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mechanistic understanding of peak current generation.

claims.claim: The failure of ECSI#6 to produce a peak current is consistent with the interpretation that this compound binds exclusively to inward-facing states.
claims.source: The failure of ECSI#6 to produce a peak current is, thus, consistent with the interpretation that this compound binds exclusively to inward-facing states.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Cocaine and noribogaine carry a charge while ECSI#6 does not.
claims.source: It should be noted, however, that cocaine and noribogaine carry a charge while ECSI#6 does not.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the chemical structures of these compounds.

claims.claim: The kapp of cocaine only increased in the very low concentration range and leveled off at about 2 s–1.
claims.source: This was not the case for cocaine (Figure 4C): as shown previously (Bulling et al., 2012), the kapp of cocaine only increased in the very low concentration range and leveled off at about 2 s–1.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4C and supported by citation to Bulling et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The binding of cocaine is limited by the return step from the inward-facing to the outward-facing state, which is the rate-limiting reaction in the transport cycle of SERT.
claims.source: This is expected for a typical inhibitor, which interacts with the outward-facing conformation of SERT, because the binding is limited by the return step from the inward-facing to the outward-facing state. This is the rate-limiting reaction in the transport cycle of SERT (Schicker et al., 2012; Hasenhuetl et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schicker et al., 2012 and Hasenhuetl et al., 2015.

claims.claim: kapp for both noribogaine and ECSI#6 increased in a linear manner as their concentrations were raised.
claims.source: In contrast, kapp for both, noribogaine (Figure 4D) and ECSI#6 (Figure 4E), increased in a linear manner as their concentrations were raised.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claims.claim: Noribogaine and ECSI#6 bind to the inward-facing conformation of SERT directly.
claims.source: This can only be achieved, if noribogaine and ECSI#6 bind to the inward-facing conformation of SERT directly.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the linear increase in kapp with concentration.

claims.claim: Noribogaine was ~10-fold more potent than ECSI#6 in imposing the block on the substrate-induced current through SERT.
claims.source: Noribogaine was ~10-fold more potent than ECSI#6 in imposing the block on the substrate-induced current through SERT.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: The kon and koff values for noribogaine were 1.7*10^5±1.6*10^4 M–1 s–1 and 1.4±0.3 s–1, respectively.
claims.source: The extracted kon and koff values were 1.7*105±1.6*104 M–1 s–1 and 1.4±0.3 s–1 and 2.1*104±3.5*103 M–1 s–1 and 1.7±0.5 s–1, for noribogaine and for ECSI#6, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: The kon and koff values for ECSI#6 were 2.1*10^4±3.5*10^3 M–1 s–1 and 1.7±0.5 s–1, respectively.
claims.source: The extracted kon and koff values were 1.7*105±1.6*104 M–1 s–1 and 1.4±0.3 s–1 and 2.1*104±3.5*103 M–1 s–1 and 1.7±0.5 s–1, for noribogaine and for ECSI#6, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: The IC50 value of ECSI#6 for blocking serotonin-induced current in the presence of 30 µM 5-HT was approximately 5 µM.
claims.source: A fit of an inhibition curve to the data points yielded an IC50 value of approx. 5 µM.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Pre-application of 100 µM ECSI#6 for 1 s or 3 s did not result in reduction of the peak current amplitude.
claims.source: We chose this time period because it had been sufficient to allow for a full current block in the other protocol (see Figure 4G): the amplitude of the peak current following the pre-application of 100 µM ECSI#6 was essentially identical to the prior control pulse. When we pre-applied 100 µM ECSI#6 for a longer period (i.e., 3 s) the amplitude of the two peak currents also remained the same (cf. lower traces in panel H).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: The lack of inhibition by ECSI#6 pre-application indicates that the affinity of ECSI#6 in the absence of 5-HT is low.
claims.source: The lack of inhibition, thus, indicates that the affinity of ECSI#6 in the absence of 5-HT is low.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: When applied from the intracellular side, ECSI#6 did not cause an appreciable current block.
claims.source: Figure 4I shows representative traces of 5-HT-induced currents recorded from SERT-expressing cells in the absence (in blue) and presence of 100 µM ECSI#6 (in red) in the electrode solution: when applied from the intracellular side, ECSI#6 did not cause an appreciable current block.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: In the ER, the folding trajectory of SERT moves through the inward-facing conformation.
claims.source: In the ER, the folding trajectory of SERT moves through the inward-facing conformation (Chiba et al., 2014; Freissmuth et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chiba et al., 2014 and Freissmuth et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Compounds which bind to the inward-facing conformation act as pharmacochaperones and rescue folding-deficient mutants of SERT and DAT.
claims.source: Compounds, which bind to the inward-facing conformation, act as pharmacochaperones: they rescue folding-deficient mutants of SERT and of DAT (Bhat et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bhat et al., 2019.

claims.claim: ECSI#6 was predicted to have pharmacochaperoning activity based on its binding to the K+-bound inward-facing state.
claims.source: Thus, ECSI#6 was predicted to have pharmacochaperoning activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the binding mode of ECSI#6.

claims.claim: SERT-PG601,602AA has a severe folding defect with the bulk of the protein trapped in the ER at an early stage of the SERT folding trajectory.
claims.source: This mutant has a severe folding defect, the bulk of the protein is trapped in the ER at an early stage of the SERT folding trajectory (El-Kasaby et al., 2010; El-Kasaby et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to El-Kasaby et al., 2010 and El-Kasaby et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Only a small fraction of SERT-PG601,602AA reaches the cell surface where it supports substrate uptake.
claims.source: Accordingly, only a small fraction of SERT-PG601,602AA reaches the cell surface, where it supports substrate uptake, but the folding defect can be corrected, if cells are preincubated with noribogaine (Bhat et al., 2021a)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bhat et al., 2021a.

claims.claim: In HEK293 cells expressing SERT-PG601,602AA, substrate uptake was only ~10% of cells expressing wild-type SERT.
claims.source: as shown in Figure 5A, in paired transient transfections, in HEK293 cells expressing SERT-PG601,602AA, substrate uptake was only ~10% of cells expressing wild-type SERT.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Preincubation of HEK293 cells with 30 µM ECSI#6 or noribogaine resulted in appreciable functional rescue of SERT-PG601,602AA, while cocaine was ineffective.
claims.source: If HEK293 cells were preincubated with 30 µM of cocaine, noribogaine or ECSI#6, appreciable functional rescue was observed with ECSI#6 and the reference compound noribogaine; cocaine was ineffective (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The pharmacochaperoning action of ECSI#6 and noribogaine was concentration-dependent and saturable.
claims.source: This pharmacochaperoning action of ECSI#6 and of noribogaine was concentration-dependent and saturable (Figure 5C)
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Noribogaine was more potent (EC50=0.46 µM) and more efficacious (Emax = 69.5%) than ECSI#6 (EC50=2.9 µM; Emax = 52%) in pharmacochaperoning SERT-PG601,602AA.

claims.claim: In the Golgi apparatus, membrane proteins incorporate additional sugar moieties to achieve mature glycosylation.

claims.claim: The band at approximately 75 kDa corresponds to the ER-resident core-glycosylated species of SERT.

claims.claim: A broad smear migrating in the range of 90–110 kDa represents the transporters carrying mature glycans.

claims.claim: Lysates from cells expressing SERT-PG601,602AA show the predominant presence of the core-glycosylated species indicating ER retention.

claims.claim: Treatment of cells expressing SERT-PG601,602AA with noribogaine or ECSI#6 for 24 hr resulted in a concentration-dependent increase in the appearance of the mature glycosylated species.

claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Noribogaine was more potent than ECSI#6 in enhancing the accumulation of mature glycosylated SERT.
claims.source: Noribogaine was more potent than ECSI#6 (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5E.

results.result: ECSI#6 is the first reported uncompetitive inhibitor of SERT, characterized by simultaneous reduction in both KM and Vmax. This uncompetitive inhibition is accounted for by preferential binding to the K+-bound inward-facing state (TiK) of SERT.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 provide direct experimental evidence of reduced KM and Vmax (Figure 3C), which is the hallmark of uncompetitive inhibition. Claims C103-C104 confirm substrate-enhanced inhibition. The mechanistic explanation (C21, C119) is supported by multiple experimental approaches (radioligand binding, electrophysiology) and kinetic modeling that converge on TiK binding.

results.result: Cocaine, noribogaine, and ECSI#6 exhibit distinct inhibition patterns: cocaine shows competitive inhibition with IC50 right-shift at higher substrate concentrations, while noribogaine and ECSI#6 show enhanced potency (left-shift) with increasing substrate, indicating fundamentally different binding modes.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C29 provide quantitative IC50 data from uptake experiments (Figure 1) showing opposite directional shifts for cocaine versus noribogaine/ECSI#6. The competitive nature of cocaine (C44) and non-competitive nature of noribogaine (C45) are supported by prior literature. The inference of different binding modes (C30-C31) logically follows from the experimental data.

results.result: Dixon plot analysis demonstrates that binding of serotonin and each inhibitor (cocaine, noribogaine, ECSI#6) to SERT is mutually exclusive, indicating they compete for overlapping binding sites despite their different inhibition mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 present experimental Dixon plot data (Figure 2D-F) showing progressive x-intercept shifts with increasing serotonin, which is the diagnostic pattern for mutually exclusive binding. The methodology (C33) is appropriately cited. This result reconciles with the uncompetitive mechanism by showing ECSI#6 binds the same site but in a different conformational state.

results.result: ECSI#6 preferentially binds K+-bound SERT with ~10-fold higher potency in 120 mM KCl versus 120 mM NaCl, contrasting with cocaine which shows the opposite preference. This demonstrates ECSI#6's selectivity for the K+-bound inward-facing state.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C42 provide quantitative radioligand binding data (Figure 2D, F) showing opposite ionic preferences for cocaine versus ECSI#6. The inference of K+-bound state preference (C43) is well-supported. Claims C37-C38 provide mechanistic context that K+ drives SERT to outward-facing states, making the preferential binding to K+-bound SERT particularly informative about ECSI#6's mechanism.

results.result: Electrophysiological recordings reveal that ECSI#6 fails to elicit peak currents and shows linear concentration-dependent increase in kapp, indicating direct binding to inward-facing SERT states. This contrasts with cocaine, which shows saturable kapp limited by the rate-limiting return step.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 provides direct experimental evidence (Figure 4A) of differential peak current generation. Claims C63-C64 show linear kapp increase for ECSI#6 (Figure 4E), supporting direct inward-facing binding. The mechanistic interpretation (C59) is appropriately cautious, noting the alternative explanation of charge differences (C60). The kinetic parameters (C66-C67) are quantitatively reported from experimental data.

results.result: ECSI#6 shows an IC50 of ~5 μM for blocking serotonin-induced current in the presence of substrate, but pre-application without substrate does not reduce peak current amplitude, indicating low affinity for SERT in the absence of substrate.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 provides quantitative IC50 from electrophysiology (Figure 4G). Claims C69-C70 present experimental evidence (Figure 4H) showing no inhibition with pre-application, supporting low affinity without substrate. This result is internally consistent with the use-dependent mechanism. Claim C71 attempts to address sidedness but appropriately acknowledges limitations in interpretation.

results.result: ECSI#6 acts as a pharmacochaperone, restoring ER export and substrate transport of the folding-deficient mutant SERT-PG601,602AA in a concentration-dependent manner (EC50=2.9 μM, Emax=52%), though less efficaciously than noribogaine.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 provide functional rescue data (Figure 5A-B) showing ECSI#6 restores transport in the mutant. Claim C79 demonstrates concentration-dependence and saturability (Figure 5C). Claim C80 provides quantitative pharmacochaperoning parameters. The prediction (C74) based on binding mode is validated by experimental results. The mechanistic basis from prior work (C75-C76) is appropriately cited.

results.result: Immunoblotting and enzymatic deglycosylation confirm that ECSI#6 and noribogaine promote concentration-dependent appearance of mature glycosylated SERT-PG601,602AA, indicating enhanced ER export, while cocaine is ineffective.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 establish the glycosylation pattern interpretation (Figure 5D) with appropriate citations. Claim C86 shows concentration-dependent increase in mature glycosylation with ECSI#6/noribogaine treatment. Claims C89-C90 provide enzymatic validation (Figure 5F) confirming band assignments. Claim C88 provides the negative control with cocaine. This biochemical evidence independently confirms the functional rescue data.

results.result: In transgenic Drosophila, oral administration of ECSI#6 or noribogaine promotes delivery of SERT-PG601,602AA to presynaptic specializations of serotonergic neurons in the fan-shaped body, demonstrating in vivo pharmacochaperoning activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 establish the experimental system showing wild-type localization versus mutant retention (Figure 6C-F). Claim C96 provides the key experimental result showing rescue with drug treatment (Figure 6G-H). Claim C98 provides the appropriate negative control. The in vivo validation (C97) strengthens the pharmacochaperoning conclusion. Prior work (C91-C92) establishes the validity of the fly model.

results.result: Saturation kinetics experiments demonstrate that cocaine causes progressive KM increase without Vmax change (competitive inhibition), noribogaine reduces Vmax without KM change (non-competitive inhibition), and ECSI#6 reduces both KM and Vmax (uncompetitive inhibition).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 provide comprehensive saturation kinetics data (Figure 3A-C) with quantitative parameters and confidence intervals. The three inhibitors show clearly distinct kinetic patterns that match their mechanistic classifications. The data quality is high with appropriate replication and statistical analysis. This result provides the definitive kinetic characterization of the three inhibition modes.

results.result: Kinetic modeling reveals that ECSI#6 binding to the TiK state with KD ~12 μM accounts for all experimental data. The IC50 shift ratio (20.6) matches the ratio of TiK occupancy at different substrate concentrations, demonstrating that substrate availability in TiK—not ECSI#6 affinity changes—drives the uncompetitive inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C151 show the modeling recapitulates experimental IC50 ratios and links this to TiK occupancy (Figure 7C-D). Claim C152 demonstrates the ratio is independent of KD variation over 3 orders of magnitude (Figure 7E), supporting the mechanistic interpretation. Claim C153 provides the estimated KD. Claims C107-C109 appropriately rule out alternative binding modes (ToNaS) based on inconsistency with experimental affinity estimates. The modeling is rigorous and well-validated.

results.result: Kinetic modeling demonstrates that noribogaine has a mixed binding mode, interacting with both ToNa and TiK states (with KD(ToNa) ~10-fold higher than KD(TiK)), explaining its intermediate inhibition pattern. This contrasts with ECSI#6, which requires KD(ToNa) 100-1000-fold higher than KD(TiK).
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126 show modeling requires dual-state binding for noribogaine, with a small uncompetitive component. Claims C154-C155 demonstrate the modeling recapitulates experimental IC50 ratios. Claims C156-C157 provide quantitative comparison showing ECSI#6's much higher selectivity for TiK. This result elegantly explains the mechanistic differences between noribogaine and ECSI#6 and resolves apparent contradictions in the literature about ibogaine/noribogaine binding.

results.result: Kinetic model simulations of substrate transport in the presence of ECSI#6 successfully recapitulate the experimental reduction in both KM and Vmax, confirming the uncompetitive inhibition mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claim C158 shows the modeling reproduces the key experimental observations from Figure 3 (shown in Figure 8B, D). This provides independent validation of the proposed mechanism through forward simulation. The agreement between simulation and experiment strengthens confidence in the TiK-binding model.

results.result: The folding trajectory of SERT in the ER visits the inward-facing conformation, and compounds binding this conformation act as pharmacochaperones. This principle is supported by second-site suppressor mutations and multiple pharmacochaperone examples.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 establish the mechanistic basis with appropriate citations. Claims C132-C134 provide supporting evidence from mutations and multiple compounds. This result provides the theoretical framework for understanding why ECSI#6's binding mode predicts pharmacochaperoning activity. The logic is sound and well-supported by prior literature.

results.result: Noribogaine shows higher pharmacochaperoning efficacy than ECSI#6. Variable efficacy among pharmacochaperones depends on both the specific mutation (stalling position in folding trajectory) and intrinsic compound properties linked to chemical structure.
results.evaluation: Claim C135 is directly supported by experimental data (Emax values). Claims C136-C139 provide literature context for variable efficacy. Claim C140 draws a reasonable inference about structure-efficacy relationships. This result provides important context for interpreting the pharmacochaperoning data and suggests directions for compound optimization.

results.result: ECSI#6's EC50 for pharmacochaperoning is lower than its IC50 for transport inhibition at saturating substrate, suggesting action on folding intermediates and making it an attractive starting point for developing pharmacochaperones with minimal transport inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claim C143 compares EC50 and IC50 values from different experimental systems, but the manuscript notes (regarding Figure 5E) that EC50 values from glycosylation differ from uptake rescue, raising questions about precision. Claim C144's inference about folding intermediates is speculative—the differential potency could reflect other factors. Claim C145 is forward-looking speculation about drug development. More rigorous comparison and mechanistic validation would be needed.

results.result: ECSI#6 is predicted to cause use-dependent block of SERT in vivo, making activated serotonergic pathways more susceptible to modulation compared to typical competitive inhibitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C148 are explicitly speculative about in vivo effects, as indicated by language like "is likely to differ" and "is predicted." While the speculation is mechanistically reasonable based on the uncompetitive mechanism, no in vivo functional data are presented to test these predictions. The fly experiments show pharmacochaperoning but not pathway-selective inhibition. This remains a hypothesis requiring experimental validation.

results.result: Background on monoamine transporters: SERT, DAT, and NET are SLC6 family members with distinct ion coupling mechanisms. They are targets for drugs ranging from non-selective (cocaine) to highly selective (SSRIs), with a continuum of ligand types including inhibitors, substrates, and pharmacochaperones. ECSI#6 is an amphetamine derivative identified as an ecstasy synthesis byproduct.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C17 provide well-established background information appropriately supported by citations to the literature. Claims C18-C19 identify ECSI#6 with appropriate citation. This contextual information is accurate and sets up the rationale for the study. All claims are either directly cited or represent established knowledge in the field.

results.result: SERT is extensively characterized with atomic structures, single-molecule studies, and real-time kinetics. Uncompetitive inhibition is rare and typically requires enzyme-substrate complex formation, but in transporters like SERT, it arises from use-dependent binding where substrate drives accumulation in the inhibitor-preferred state (TiK).
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 establish SERT's extensive characterization with appropriate citations. Claims C105-C106 define uncompetitive inhibition in enzymes. Claims C114-C115 provide the ion channel analogy. Claims C116-C118 explain the mechanism in SERT. This result synthesizes background knowledge and mechanistic interpretation to explain how uncompetitive inhibition operates in a transporter context, which differs from the classical enzyme mechanism.

results.result: Discussion of mechanistic principles: Ibogaine/noribogaine bind from the extracellular side to trap inward-facing SERT. The outward- and inward-facing conformations are equivalent stable folds. ER ionic conditions favor inward-facing conformations. Four pharmacochaperoning mechanisms exist, but aggregate-related mechanisms don't apply to SERT.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C124 discuss ibogaine binding with appropriate citations, resolving apparent contradictions. Claims C127, C129-C131 discuss conformational equilibria and ER conditions with citations. Claims C141-C142 discuss pharmacochaperoning mechanisms. All claims are well-supported by literature and provide important context for interpreting the results. This represents synthesis of established knowledge rather than new findings.
